title: Linked Lists
definition: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements are not stored at contiguous memory locations. Each element (node) contains a data field and a reference (link) to the next node in the sequence.
conceptExplanation: Linked lists solve the fixed-size limitation of arrays. Each node contains data and a pointer to the next node. This allows dynamic size and efficient insertion/deletion, but does not support random access.
keyPoints: - Nodes contain data and next pointer - Dynamic size - No random access - Insertion/deletion at any position is O(1) if pointer is known
importantTerminology: Node, Head, Next, Null, Pointer, Traversal, Insertion, Deletion
workingPrinciple: Each node has two fields: data and next. The next field points to the next node. The last node points to null. Traversal starts from head and follows next pointers until null.
realLifeExample: Music playlist, undo/redo functionality in editors, dynamic memory allocation
dsaExample: Inserting a node at the beginning, deleting a node at a given position, reversing a linked list
algorithm:
Linked List Traversal:
1. Set current = head
2. While current != null:
   - Process current.data
   - Move current = current.next
3. End while
pseudocode:
BEGIN
  SET current = head
  WHILE current != NULL
    PROCESS current.data
    SET current = current.next
  END WHILE
END
complexity: Time: Access O(n), Insertion at beginning O(1), Deletion by key O(n), Search O(n)\nSpace: O(n) for n nodes
applications: Dynamic memory allocation, playlist management, hash table collision resolution, stack/queue implementation
advantages: Dynamic size, efficient insertion/deletion no need to shift elements, memory efficiency
limitations: No random access, extra memory for pointers, sequential access only
commonMistakes: Losing the head reference, not setting next to null, memory leaks from circular references
importantExamPoints: Difference between singly, doubly, and circular linked lists, node structure, traversal algorithms, time complexity comparison with arrays

fiveMarkQuestions.question: Explain singly linked list with its operations and complexity.
fiveMarkQuestions.answer: A singly linked list consists of nodes where each node has a data field and a next pointer pointing to the next node. The last node points to null. Operations include: - Insertion at beginning/end/given position - Deletion by key/position - Traversal - Search. Insertion/deletion at beginning is O(1), at end/given position is O(n) without tail pointer, O(1) with tail pointer. Search and deletion by key are O(n). Advantages: dynamic size, no need to shift elements. Disadvantages: no random access, extra memory for pointers.

tenMarkQuestions.question: Explain singly linked list with all operations, algorithms, and applications in detail.
tenMarkQuestions.answer:
A singly linked list is a linear data structure composed of nodes. Each node contains data and a reference (link) to the next node in the sequence. The first node is called the head, and the last node points to null. 

Operations:
- Traversal: Start from head, follow next pointers until null. Time: O(n).
- Insertion at beginning: Create new node, set its next to head, update head. Time: O(1).
- Insertion at end: If tail pointer exists, O(1); otherwise traverse to end O(n).
- Deletion by key: Search for node, update previous.next to skip the node. Time: O(n).
- Search: Compare each node's data with target. Time: O(n).

Applications: Dynamic memory allocation, implementing stacks/queues, hash table chaining, polynomial representation.

Comparison with arrays: Arrays provide O(1) random access but O(n) insertion/deletion. Linked lists provide O(1) insertion/deletion (at known position) but O(n) access.

Memory representation: Each node is dynamically allocated. The head pointer stores the address of the first node. Free memory management requires proper deletion to avoid memory leaks.
